Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA UK weather Homes damaged as storms follow heatwaves in England and Wales Environment Agency issues 40 flood alerts across Midlands, Yorkshire and south-east of England Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent Thu 27 Aug 2026 11.41 EDT First published on Thu 27 Aug 2026 10.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Dozens of homes have been damaged by flooding and the Met Office had issued warnings for thunderstorms and heavy rain at the end of a summer in which most of England and the whole of Wales was declared in drought. The Met Office said thundery showers in England and Wales could cause 75mm of rain to fall in just 12 hours in some areas. The Environment Agency (EA) issued 40 flood alerts, where flooding is possible, across the Midlands, Yorkshire and the south-east on Thursday morning. A flood alert was issued for the River Maun at Edwinstowe and Ollerton in Nottinghamshire. The EA said river levels at Mansfield The Dykes gauging station were rising rapidly due to the nature of the catchment, and Old Rufford Road was most at risk. A yellow thunderstorm warning for parts of the Midlands, east of England, south of England, the north-west, Yorkshire and Humber and Wales is in place until 10pm on Thursday. View image in fullscreen A road in Birmingham becomes flooded after the River Tame, which runs under the road, burst its banks. Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News. A second yellow warning for Lincolnshire, parts of the east of England, parts of Yorkshire, Kent and Medway will be in place from 5pm on Thursday to 7am on Friday. Climate scientists have repeatedly warned that global heating is causing more volatile weather patterns in the UK, with intense heatwaves, droughts, flooding and storms. Five heatwaves have been recorded in the UK this summer. A Birmingham man whose property was damaged in thunderstorms on Wednesday night described seeing a “river coming around the corner” before his home was flooded. Areas of Birmingham saw significant flooding on Wednesday after the EA issued a flood warning for the Perry Barr area. Staffordshire, where a lower-level flood alert is in place, had 60mm of rainfall in 12 hours, according to the Environment Agency. West Midlands fire service was alerted to flooding at 32 properties near the Tame Valley canal on Wednesday evening and sent seven fire engines to the scene. View image in fullscreen Commuters holding umbrellas cross London Bridge. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA Ryan Goodwin, who lives on one of the affected streets, said his conservatory was flooded with 3ft (1 metre) of water and his living room was damaged. He said: “About 7.30pm I got home, I was in the car with the kids and I thought I don’t want to get out yet, there’s too many puddles here. Then in a matter of about half an hour it was just a river coming round the corner, all the way down the road.” Describing the damage to his home to the Press Association, he said: “It’s gone under the laminate flooring in the front room. The conservatory got flooded, the electrics went off. The conservatory had about 3ft of water – luckily that is below the house level. “The neighbours’ carpet and sofa and everything got wet as well. Down the road they have two hills running into the corner, it was halfway up their doors, so I think we got a bit lucky here, really.” Goodwin, who lives near the M6, said he was not sure how long it would take to repair his home. “I’m just trying to get everything out that is wet and speak to the insurance at the moment,” he said. “All the water comes off the motorway as well. It has been so dry for so long, all the leaves had blocked the drains and everything. Hopefully it doesn’t happen again.” Goodwin’s father-in-law, Jay Patel, said: “[The water] was really, really fast. I couldn’t believe how fast it was.” View image in fullscreen Rain falls on parched ground after a succession of heatwaves in England and Wales. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock The EA said after a National Drought Group meeting on Thursday morning that 71.3% of England remained in drought. It said only 34% of the rainfall typically expected in August had been received so far. The agency’s chief executive, Philip Duffy, said: “A few days or even weeks of wetter weather cannot reverse the impacts of several months of exceptionally dry conditions. Today’s yellow thunderstorm warnings show it’s possible to experience simultaneous drought and flood as heavy rain falls on compacted soils.” Explore more on these topics UK weather West Midlands Birmingham England news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Matt Roberts/Shutterstock New York Analysis Mamdani’s nuanced plan offers a roadmap to tackle antisemitism – and reignites criticism of the mayor Alice Speri in New York Critics noted that the plan does not discuss Israel; others praised it for not conflating Jews with the state of Israel Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 08.02 EDT Share When the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, announced the city’s first-ever municipal strategy to address antisemitism – a nuanced, multi-pronged approach ranging from greater security measures for synagogues to an increased focus on Jewish history in public school education – critics were quick to note what the 33-page document does not mention at all: Israel. Israel has played an outsized role in Mamdani’s campaign and since his election, with the mayor standing by his years-long support for Palestinians, and frequently describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a war criminal. His positions have split New York’s Jewish communities , and earned him frequent accusations that he is fomenting the very antisemitism he has pledged to fight. At the United Nations general assembly last week, Netanyahu – who is wanted for war crimes and crimes against humanity by the international criminal court (ICC) and whom Mamdani had at one point pledged to arrest – called him “the antisemitic mayor of New York”. View image in fullscreen Benjamin Netanyahu’s notes mentioning Mamdani sit on the podium as he addresses the 81st UN general assembly in New York last week. Photograph: Jeenah Moon/Reuters Mamdani has gone to great lengths to engage with representatives of New York’s many Jewish communities and the antisemitism strategy, several of them said, reflects those conversations and the mayor’s willingness to listen to those communities’ concerns. “This strategy is an important intervention that reflects the voices of the hundreds of Jewish New Yorkers consulted throughout the process, that celebrates the diversity and vibrancy of Jewish New Yorkers, and that commits real city resources to fighting antisemitism wherever it appears,” Rabbi Jill Jacobs, chief executive of T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, said in a statement. Still, many of the critiques hinge on an absence: Mamdani’s strategy does not endorse a specific definition of antisemitism, the subject of many disputes largely stemming over the centrality of Israel to Jewishness. Instead it mentions three different ones while noting that “New York City can and will leverage all of the tools at its disposal to combat antisemitism effectively without needing to adopt a definition for this specific form of hate”. Federal hate crimes statutes, the strategy notes, also do not adopt a standalone definition of discrimination. Instead, the strategy, which was announced on Tuesday, cites extensive polling capturing how Jewish Americans feel about safety and antisemitism and notes the diversity of ways in which they experience antisemitism. “These experiences are shaped by individual perception, context and a person’s sense of safety, and may vary from person to person while still reflecting real concerns felt more broadly across communities,” the strategy notes. The document adds that New York police have reported a “notable increase” of anti-Jewish crimes in the three years since the 7 October Hamas attacks in Israel and its subsequent war in Gaza, and references a string of antisemitic incidents across the country going back years, including the attack on the Tree of Life Synagogue in Pittsburgh, which killed 11 people in 2018. While Jews make up 12% of the city’s population, antisemitic crimes make up more than half of all hate crimes, the mayor said in a video introducing the strategy. “This is not only unacceptable, it’s something we all have an obligation to change,” Mamdani said. The plan has reignited criticism of the mayor – from both pro-Israel and pro-Palestine camps. A coalition of Jewish organizations and the New York board of rabbis wrote in a joint statement that the strategy “fails to address a central issue that the Mayor himself has perpetuated: rhetoric that demonizes and delegitimizes Israel inevitably leads to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers”. Meanwhile, some of the left have also been unhappy with the plan. “One loud camp is (predictably) saying that Mamdani’s antisemitism plan is not Zionist enough, while another is claiming it’s (somehow) too Zionist,” noted Ben Lorber, an analyst who researches antisemitism. “Of course, the issue of antisemitism is overdetermined today by Israel/Palestine. But at root this is a municipal hate crimes prevention strategy. Nobody benefits by obsessively reading it through the [Israel/Palestine] prism.” Those who praised the plan saw the omission of Israel as a welcome and deliberate effort to separate what has so often been conflated: antisemitism and criticism of Israel, which can veer into antisemitism but is not that by default. Mamdani’s plan “makes it really clear that Israel is not a synonym for Jew”, Lila Corwin Berman, director of the center for American Jewish history at New York University, said. “Jews are not the same as Israel. “In a very material way it is resisting what I think is a vector of antisemitism, which is the conflation of Jews with the state of Israel, which tends to produce some awfully antisemitic kinds of actions.” She added: “If there is a sort of downside to it, I think it might be that it takes some critical thinking skills to understand why they’re approaching the topic in the way they did and not foregrounding Israel and Zionism.” Still, she said: “Some people, they feel as if Mamdani’s views on Israel are disqualifying.” Mamdani’s plan came just a day after the US commission on civil rights, a bipartisan federal agency tasked with monitoring civil rights enforcement, issued a 220-page report on campus antisemitism . The report analyzed how anti-discrimination protections enshrined in the Civil Rights Act apply to campus antisemitism and drew a distinction – collapsed by both the Trump administration and many universities – between conduct “motivated by hostility toward people of Jewish ancestry as such” and speech criticizing “ideas or institutions” such as Israel or Zionism. “The report makes clear that the former can constitute discrimination under the Civil Rights Act, while the latter generally cannot,” said Amanda Shanor, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who has written about the Trump administration’s instrumenatlization of antisemitism charges. “The report explains that rallies, chants and protests directed at a campus community as a whole also generally do not constitute the type of targeted discrimination or harassment that is actionable under civil rights laws.” Mamdani’s plan offers a roadmap for municipal efforts to tackle antisemitism, and the commission’s report offers a legal framework for universities addressing campus antisemitism while respecting free expression, freedom of assembly, and academic freedom. But the two documents offer nuanced interventions, informed by a diversity of perspectives, in a debate that has been largely flattened amid heated political rhetoric, said Jonathan Jacoby, the president of the Nexus Project, a Jewish group dedicated to combating antisemitism and upholding free speech. “Some institutions and individuals are going to just see it as an opportunity to continue to bash Mamdani for reasons that have to do more with their own opinions about Israel than they have to do with antisemitism,” he added. “Mamdani’s strategy respects the complexity of the issue, and there are those who will try to dumb down the issue and flatten the complexity.” Explore more on these topics New York Zohran Mamdani US politics Antisemitism Israel analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
